title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Criminals used AI-generated video and deepfake technology to impersonate a real immigration attorney on social media, creating hundreds of fake accounts offering fraudulent legal services. The scam targeted vulnerable immigrants seeking residency assistance, directing victims to communicate through WhatsApp and payment apps after exchanging fake contracts. This is a case of AI-enabled impersonation deployed at scale across social platforms without verification of identity by the platforms themselves.

The failure occurred in the deployment of generative AI tools by bad actors, not in a legitimate AI system. What would have caught this earlier: social media platforms implementing verification systems for professionals offering services, or human review of accounts making legal service claims before they accumulate followers and process payments. The scale of the fraud, with nearly 6,500 accounts removed across platforms, suggests these verification checks were not in place.

It is not established whether the social media platforms were negligent in their moderation, whether they received adequate notice before the anti-piracy company's intervention, or what technical measures might have automatically detected the deepfakes as synthetic media.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos using his likeness to offer fraudulent immigration services, including US residency assistance for $2,200. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began contacting his office after seeing these videos on social media platforms.

The fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months, prompting Leal to hire an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scammers typically direct people to WhatsApp, exchange fake contracts, and request payment through digital payment apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams. He advises immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be wary of social media advertisements requesting immediate payment.
